title: How to Speak English Fluently: A Realistic Plan
excerpt: Everyone wants to speak English fluently, but most advice is either vague ("just practise!") or sells a shortcut that doesn't exist. Here's the honest version. Fluency means…
author: Salma Saleem

blocks.text: Everyone wants to speak English fluently, but most advice is either vague ("just practise!") or sells a shortcut that doesn't exist. Here's the honest version. Fluency means communicating your ideas smoothly and confidently — not speaking perfectly. It's built mainly by speaking out loud every day, not by studying more grammar. There's no magic method and no overnight result, but there is a clear, realistic path that works for anyone who follows it consistently.

This is that plan: what fluency actually is, the five things that build it, how long it really takes, and the myths that slow people down. Each section links to a deeper guide if you want to go further.
What fluency really means
Fluency is the ability to express your ideas smoothly and keep a conversation going, without long pauses or getting stuck. It's about flow.
It is not: Perfect grammar — fluent speakers make small mistakes all the time. A native accent — you can be fully fluent with a strong accent.
Knowing every word — fluent speakers simply talk around words they don't know. Speaking fast — clarity and flow matter more than speed.
This reframe matters because chasing perfection is what keeps people silent. Once you aim for communicating well instead of speaking perfectly, fluency gets much closer — and far less stressful.
The 5 pillars of fluency

Fluency rests on five things working together. Neglect one and progress stalls. 1. Input — listen a lot. Podcasts, shows, and conversations feed your brain the words, rhythm, and patterns you'll later produce. Input fuels output.

Output — speak every day. This is the pillar most people skip, and it's the most important. You get fluent at what you practise, so you must actually talk out loud, daily. (See daily English speaking practice.) 3. Think in English. Stop translating from your first language; go straight from idea to English so you can speak in real time. (See how to think in English.) 4. Build vocabulary in chunks. Learn ready-made phrases, not just single words, so you can grab whole blocks of language instantly. This is what makes speech flow. 5. Confidence. Fluency and confidence feed each other — you speak more when you're not afraid, and you get more fluent the more you speak. (See how to build confidence speaking English.) If you feel stuck despite studying for years, it's almost always pillar 2 that's missing: you understand English (strong input) but rarely speak it (weak output). (See why you understand English but can't speak it.)
A realistic timeline

Fluency is gradual, and "how long" depends on your starting level and how much you practise. But here's a realistic shape of the journey with consistent daily speaking: Stage What it feels like Rough focus

Hesitant You understand but freeze and translate a lot Start speaking daily, even alone There's no fixed number of weeks — anyone promising "fluent in 30 days" is selling something. What's reliable is the direction: daily speaking moves you up these stages steadily, and most learners feel a real difference within a few months of consistent practice.
Myths that slow you down
"More grammar will make me fluent." Grammar study helps accuracy, but fluency comes from speaking. You can know every rule and still freeze.
"I'll speak once I'm ready." You never feel ready — confidence comes from speaking, not before it. Start now, at your current level.

"I must avoid mistakes." Mistakes are how you improve. Avoiding them means avoiding speaking, which is the opposite of what builds fluency. "I need to sound like a native." You don't. Clear, confident, accented English is fully fluent.
"I can get fluent just by watching shows." Input helps, but without output you'll understand far more than you can say.
Almost every myth points the same way: they keep you not speaking. The fix is always to speak more.

Putting it together: a weekly plan A simple way to work all five pillars in a week: Daily (15 min): speak out loud — narrate, answer a question, or have a conversation. This is non-negotiable; it's pillar 2.
Daily (10–15 min): input — listen to a podcast or watch a show in English. A few times a week: learn and reuse 3–5 new chunks out loud.
Ongoing: think in English during small daily moments, and track your speaking streak to build confidence.
Stage What it feels like Rough focus

Emerging You can hold simple conversations with pauses Build confidence and reduce translating Conversational You chat comfortably on familiar topics Expand topics, add chunks and nuance Fluent You express ideas smoothly, mistakes and all Polish, tackle harder topics The whole plan lives or dies on daily speaking. The hardest part is having someone to speak to — which is where an AI speaking partner like Yappply helps: a daily conversation on any topic, judgment-free, with live corrections and a progress report, so the output pillar actually happens every day. Get that daily speaking habit going and the other pillars fall into place around it. Fluency isn't a secret method — it's showing up to speak, a little, every day.
Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to become fluent in English? It depends on your starting level and daily practice, but with consistent daily speaking most learners feel a real difference within a few months. Fluency is gradual — anyone promising it in 30 days is overselling. What's the fastest way to become fluent in English? Speak out loud every day. Output is the pillar most learners skip, and it's the one that builds fluency fastest. Pair daily speaking with regular listening and growing confidence.

Do I need perfect grammar to be fluent? No. Fluency is about communicating smoothly and confidently; fluent speakers make small mistakes constantly. Chasing perfect grammar actually slows fluency because it makes you hesitate.

Can I become fluent without living in an English-speaking country? Yes. Daily speaking practice, English input, and thinking in English can be done anywhere, especially with AI conversation tools that give you a partner on demand.

Why am I not fluent even though I understand English well? Because understanding (input) and speaking (output) are different skills. If you rarely speak, your output lags behind. The fix is daily speaking practice.

title: How to Introduce Yourself in a Job Interview in English
excerpt: "Tell me about yourself" is almost always the first question in a job interview — and it sets the tone for everything after. Most candidates either freeze or ramble for three…
author: Salma Saleem

blocks.text: "Tell me about yourself" is almost always the first question in a job interview — and it sets the tone for everything after. Most candidates either freeze or ramble for three minutes about their life story.

Here's the fix: answer in 45–90 seconds using a simple Present → Past → Future structure — what you do now, the relevant experience that led here, and why you're excited about this role. It's not a biography and it's not your whole CV read aloud; it's a short, focused snapshot that gives the interviewer a reason to keep listening. This guide gives you the structure, two example answers, the mistakes to avoid, and how to practise so it comes out naturally on the day.
What interviewers actually want

When an interviewer says "tell me about yourself," they're not asking for your hobbies or where you grew up. They're really asking: why should we keep listening, and why do you fit this role? It's a positioning question.

A strong answer does three things: it shows you can summarise your value clearly, it stays relevant to the job, and it gives the interviewer a hook — something specific they'll want to ask more about. Keep it professional and tied to the role; save personal details unless they're directly relevant.

For English learners, there's a bonus: a calm, well-structured opening answer signals confidence and fluency straight away, which makes a strong first impression even if the rest of your English isn't perfect.
The Present → Past → Future formula
This simple three-part structure keeps you focused and easy to follow. Prepare the shape, not a word-for-word script.

Present — what you do now. Start with your current role and a one-line summary of what you do. "I'm currently a [role] at [company], where I [main responsibility]." If you're a student or between jobs: "I recently graduated in [field]" or "I've spent the last year building skills in [area]."

Past — the relevant experience that led here. Give one or two achievements or experiences that connect to this job. "Before that, I [experience], where I [specific result]." Pick what's relevant to the role, not your whole history. 3. Future — why you're here, now. Connect yourself to this role and company. "I'm looking to [goal], which is why this role at [company] really interests me — I'd love to [contribution]."

Useful phrases to link the parts: currently, before that, prior to this, over the past few years, which is why, I'm particularly excited about… These connectors make your answer flow and sound coherent.
Two example answers
Use these as models for the structure — then swap in your own details. Don't memorise them word for word.

Experienced professional (applying for a marketing role): "I'm currently a digital marketing executive at a retail company, where I run our social media and email campaigns. Before that, I worked at a small agency managing content for three different clients, and one campaign I led grew a client's followers by about 40% in six months. I've really enjoyed the creative side of the work, and I'm now looking to take on bigger brand projects — which is exactly why this marketing role at your company caught my eye. I'd love to bring that campaign experience to a bigger team."

Fresh graduate / career-changer: "I recently graduated with a degree in business administration, and during my studies I did a six-month internship in customer support, where I learned how to handle people and solve problems under pressure. I also led a final-year group project, which taught me a lot about teamwork and meeting deadlines. I'm now excited to start my career in a customer-focused role, and this position really appeals to me because it combines communication with problem-solving — two things I genuinely enjoy." Notice that both are under 90 seconds, stay relevant to the role, and end by connecting to the job.
Common mistakes to avoid
Rambling for too long. Three-minute answers lose the interviewer. Keep it to 45–90 seconds and stop.
Reciting your whole CV. They have your resume. Pick only the one or two most relevant things, not a chronological list of every job.

Starting with personal life. Age, family, hometown, and hobbies aren't what they asked for. Stay professional unless something is directly relevant to the role. Sounding memorised and robotic. A script delivered in a flat voice is obvious and off- putting. Learn the structure so you can speak it naturally, a little differently each time. Being too generic. "I'm hardworking and a team player" says nothing. Use a specific example or result instead — it's more believable and more memorable. Not connecting to the job. If your answer would fit any role at any company, it's too vague. Always end by tying yourself to this role.
Practise until it sounds natural

Knowing the structure isn't enough — the difference between freezing and sounding confident is practice out loud. Prepare your Present-Past-Future points, then say your answer aloud many times, slightly differently each time, until it feels natural rather than recited. Record yourself and check: is it under 90 seconds? Does it sound like you, or like a script? Do you connect to the role at the end?

The best practice is a realistic mock interview where you're asked the question and have to respond on the spot — but most people don't have someone to run mocks with. An AI speaking partner lets you rehearse your self-introduction and other interview questions as many times as you want, out loud, and gives you instant feedback on your fluency, grammar, and pronunciation. If you have an interview coming up, practising your answer aloud with an AI partner a few times beforehand is the single best way to walk in calm and confident.
Frequently asked questions

How do I answer "tell me about yourself" in an interview? Use the Present-Past-Future structure: what you do now, the relevant experience that led here, and why you're excited about this role. Keep it to 45–90 seconds and end by connecting to the job. How long should my self-introduction be? Around 45 to 90 seconds. Long enough to give a clear snapshot, short enough to keep the interviewer engaged and leave them wanting to ask more.

Should I memorise my answer? No. Memorised answers sound robotic and interviewers can tell. Learn the structure and your key points, then practise saying it naturally so it's a little different each time.

What should I not include in my introduction? Avoid your life story, personal details like age or family, your full job history, and vague clichés like "hardworking team player." Keep it professional, specific, and relevant to the role.

How can I practise introducing myself in English? Write your Present-Past-Future points, then say your answer out loud repeatedly — ideally in a mock interview with a partner or an AI speaking partner that asks the question and gives feedback on your delivery.

title: How to Improve English Pronunciation (Without a Teacher)
excerpt: Good news first: you don't need a teacher or a native accent to have clear English pronunciation. The goal isn't to erase your accent — it's to be easily understood — and you can…
author: Salma Saleem

blocks.text: Good news first: you don't need a teacher or a native accent to have clear English pronunciation. The goal isn't to erase your accent — it's to be easily understood — and you can train that yourself with a simple listen, imitate, and record loop. An accent is completely fine; millions of people speak clear, professional English with one. What matters is clarity: the right sounds, stress, and rhythm so listeners never have to work to understand you. This guide covers what actually affects clarity, how to practise each part alone, and the sounds most learners need to target.
What pronunciation really is

Pronunciation isn't just individual sounds — it's four things, and some matter more than others for being understood: Individual sounds. The consonants and vowels, like the th in "think" or the difference between "ship" and "sheep." Important, but not the whole story.

Word stress. Which syllable you emphasise in a word (PHO-to-graph vs pho-TOG-ra- pher). Getting this wrong confuses listeners more than a slightly off sound does. Sentence stress and rhythm. English stresses the important words (nouns, verbs) and reduces the small ones (a, the, of). This rhythm is what makes speech sound natural.
Intonation. The rise and fall of your voice — rising for questions, falling for statements. It carries meaning and emotion.
For clarity, word and sentence stress usually matter most. Many learners obsess over perfecting single sounds when fixing their stress and rhythm would make them far easier to understand.
How to practise alone

You don't need a teacher — you need your ears, your voice, and a way to record. These techniques do the job: 1. Shadowing. Play a short clip of a native speaker and speak along with them, copying their sounds, stress, and rhythm as closely as you can. It's the single most effective self-practice for pronunciation.

Record and compare. Record yourself saying a sentence, then play the original and your version back to back. Your ear will catch the difference your mouth missed. 3. Minimal pairs. Practise word pairs that differ by one sound — ship/sheep, three/tree, very/berry. This trains you to hear and produce the exact sounds you struggle with. 4. Exaggerate your mouth movement. Open your mouth more and over-pronounce when practising. It builds the muscle memory so your normal speech becomes clearer. 5. Learn word stress as you learn words. When you note a new word, mark which syllable is stressed and say it out loud. Correct stress is often more important than perfect sounds.
Target your problem sounds. Don't practise everything — find the two or three sounds that actually trip you up and drill those. (For general clarity drills, see our articulation guide.)
Common problem areas

Which sounds are hard depends on your first language, but these trip up many English learners: The "th" sounds (think, this) — often swapped for t, d, s, or z. Put your tongue lightly between your teeth.

V vs W (vest vs west) — V uses your top teeth on your bottom lip; W rounds your lips. Word endings — many learners drop final consonants ("wan" for "want"). Fully finishing words is a quick clarity win.
Consonant clusters (strengths, asked, scripts) — practise them slowly, then speed up.
R and L — which is harder depends on your language; minimal pairs (right/light) help. Word stress on longer words — putting the stress on the wrong syllable is a common source of being misunderstood.
Focus only on the ones that actually cause you trouble — recording yourself will quickly reveal which they are.
A 10-minute daily routine
Consistency wins here too — 10 minutes a day beats an hour once a week. Within a few weeks, the sounds you drilled start showing up correctly in your normal speech.
The one thing self-practice misses

The limit of practising alone is your own ear: you can't always hear which sounds you're getting wrong, because they sound right to you. A teacher's job is to catch those and point them out. Yappply gives you that feedback without a teacher — as you talk to your AI partner, it flags the words and sounds that came out unclearly, so you know exactly what to fix instead of guessing. Combined with daily shadowing and recording, that instant feedback is what makes self-taught pronunciation actually improve. If you want clearer pronunciation but don't have a teacher to tell you what's off, an AI partner that listens and corrects is the closest thing to one.
Minutes What to do What it trains

0–3 Shadow a short clip of a native speaker Sounds, stress, and rhythm together 3–5 Drill 5 minimal pairs for your problem sound Hearing and producing tricky sounds 5–7 Read a paragraph aloud, exaggerating mouth movement and marking stressed words Clarity and word stress
7–9 Record yourself and compare to the original Catching your own errors 9–10 Pick one word you got wrong and say it correctly 10 times Fixing it for good
Frequently asked questions

Can I improve my English pronunciation without a teacher? Yes. Shadowing native speakers, recording and comparing yourself, drilling minimal pairs, and learning word stress all work on your own. The main thing a teacher adds is feedback — which an AI speaking app can now provide.

Do I need to lose my accent to speak clearly? No. The goal is to be easily understood, not to sound native. Plenty of people speak clear, professional English with an accent. Focus on clarity — sounds, stress, and rhythm — not erasing your accent.

What matters most for clear pronunciation? Word stress and sentence rhythm usually matter most for being understood — often more than perfecting individual sounds. Fix your stress and you'll be clearer immediately.

What is shadowing and why does it work? Shadowing is speaking along with a native speaker in real time, copying their sounds and rhythm. It trains sounds, stress, and intonation together, which is why it's the most effective self-practice technique. How long does it take to improve pronunciation? With daily practice, most learners notice clearer speech within a few weeks, especially on the specific sounds and stress patterns they target. It's gradual but steady.

title: How to Improve Your Articulation: 3 Exercises for Clearer, Crisper Speech
excerpt: You know the feeling. You say something in a meeting or a conversation, and the other person leans in and asks, "Sorry, what was that?" Your English might be grammatically…
author: Salma Saleem

blocks.text: Why clear articulation changes how people hear you

You know the feeling. You say something in a meeting or a conversation, and the other person leans in and asks, "Sorry, what was that?" Your English might be grammatically perfect, your vocabulary wide, your ideas sharp — but if the words come out soft, rushed, or swallowed, none of that lands.

That is an articulation problem, not an English problem. And the good news is that articulation is a physical skill, like any other. It is trained by movement and repetition, not by memorising more rules. In this guide you will learn what articulation actually is, why mumbling happens, and three simple exercises you can practise in ten minutes a day to speak more clearly and sound more confident in English.
None of these exercises require a teacher, an app, or any equipment. You only need your own mouth and a few minutes of focused practice.
What articulation really is (and why you mumble)

Articulation is how clearly you shape each sound with your lips, tongue, and jaw. Think of your mouth as the instrument and your words as the music. When the instrument barely moves, the notes blur together.

Mumbling is rarely about shyness or a "bad voice." It usually comes down to two habits: 1. Lazy mouth movement. Most people barely open their mouths when they speak. The lips and jaw stay almost still, so consonants lose their edges and words run into each other.
Low or fading energy. Many speakers start a sentence strong and let it collapse by the end, so the final words come out weak and muddy.

Fix those two things and your clarity improves immediately — no accent coaching required. The three exercises below target exactly these habits. Exercise 1: over-articulate on purpose The fastest way to sound crisper is to deliberately exaggerate your mouth movements. Open your mouth wider than feels normal, stretch each vowel, and hit every consonant hard. It will feel theatrical — almost silly. That feeling is the point. You are not trying to talk like this in real life. You are building muscle memory so that your "normal" setting becomes clearer than it is today. Athletes train with heavier weights than they use in a game; this is the same idea for your mouth.
How to practise it
Pick any book, article, or script in English.
Read it aloud for five minutes, over-articulating every single word. Exaggerate the lip and jaw movement so much that it almost aches. Do this once a day.

After a week or two, drop back to normal speech. You will notice your everyday articulation has sharpened on its own, because your mouth is now used to moving more. Exercise 2: keep your energy to the end of every sentence Listen closely to most speakers and you will hear the same pattern: the first few words are clear, then the voice trails off and the ending turns into a low, crackly mumble. That crackle is often called vocal fry, and it happens when you run out of breath and energy before you run out of sentence.
The fix is to give every word in a sentence the same level of energy — the last word as strong and clear as the first.
A simple drill: Count out loud from one to ten.
Give each number exactly the same energy, volume, and clarity.
Record yourself and check: does "ten" sound as strong as "one"? Or did you fade after "six"?
Repeat until the energy is flat and even across all ten.
Once even counting feels natural, apply it to full sentences. Finishing strong instantly makes you sound more confident and in control, and it stops your endings from dissolving into mush.

Exercise 3: open up to remove nasality A nasal, pinched tone makes even clear words sound thin and less pleasant to listen to. It usually happens when the sound is trapped up in the nose instead of flowing out through an open, relaxed mouth.

You do not need complex vocal techniques to fix this. In most cases, nasality fades on its own once you combine the first two exercises: open your mouth more (Exercise 1) and carry full, even energy through the whole sentence (Exercise 2). An open, energised mouth naturally pushes the sound forward and out rather than up and in. Try this: Say a sentence the way you normally would and notice where the sound sits. Now say it again with your mouth open wider and steady energy on every word. Feel the sound shift from your nose to the front of your mouth.
The result is a rounder, warmer, clearer voice — without you having to think about your nose at all.
Your 10-minute daily articulation routine
You do not need hours. Consistency beats intensity. Here is a simple routine that folds all three exercises into ten minutes a day: Minutes What to do Focus
0–5 Read a book or article aloud, over-articulating every word Mouth movement (Exercise

1) That last minute matters most. Recording yourself and listening back is the single fastest way to hear what others hear — and to catch the exact words where you fade or mumble. Practise out loud, every day Articulation only improves when you actually speak — out loud, regularly, with feedback. Reading silently or memorising tips will not move your mouth muscles. The speakers who sound clear and confident are simply the ones who put in reps.

The hard part for most learners is having something (or someone) to practise with every day, and getting honest feedback on where they mumble or fade. That is exactly where talking to an AI speaking partner helps: you get a daily conversation to practise on, and instant feedback on your clarity, pacing, and energy — without the fear of being judged. If you want to turn these exercises into a daily habit, practising your speaking with an AI partner is one of the easiest ways to stay consistent and actually hear your progress.
Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to improve articulation? Most people notice a difference within one to two weeks of daily five-minute practice. The over-articulation habit builds quickly because it is pure muscle memory.
Is mumbling the same as having an accent? No. An accent is how you pronounce sounds; mumbling is how clearly you produce them. You can have any accent and still speak with crisp, clear articulation.

Can I improve articulation without a coach? Yes. All three exercises here are self- directed. The only thing you really need is a way to hear yourself — so record your practice or use an AI speaking partner for instant feedback.

Why do my sentences trail off at the end? Usually because your energy and breath fade before the sentence does. Practise finishing every sentence with the same energy you started it with (Exercise 2).
Minutes What to do Focus
5–7 Count 1–10 with identical energy, then say five sentences finishing each one strong Even energy (Exercise 2)
7–9 Re-read one paragraph with an open mouth and steady energy Removing nasality (Exercise

3) 9–10 Record a short clip of yourself speaking freely and listen back Self-feedback What should I read aloud for practice? Anything in English you enjoy — a news article, a book, a blog post, even product reviews. The content does not matter; the exaggerated mouth movement does.

title: English Phrases for Phone and Video Calls at Work
excerpt: Phone and video calls in English are harder than talking face-to-face — and it's not just you. Without body language to help, and with audio that can cut out, calls demand…
author: Salma Saleem

blocks.text: Phone and video calls in English are harder than talking face-to-face — and it's not just you. Without body language to help, and with audio that can cut out, calls demand clearer, more structured language. The fix is to have ready phrases for each predictable moment: starting the call, handling audio problems, taking turns, and wrapping up. This is especially useful for remote and call-centre work, where most of your English happens over a line. Learn the phrases below, and calls stop being something to dread and become routine.
Starting a call
Answering the phone: "Hello, this is [name] speaking."
"[Company], [name] speaking — how can I help you?"
Making a call / introducing yourself
"Hi, this is [name] from [company]. Is now a good time to talk?" "I'm calling about…" "Could I speak to [name], please?"
Joining a video call: "Hi everyone, can you hear me okay?"
"Sorry I'm a minute late — thanks for waiting."
"Let me just turn my camera on."
Small talk to open
"Thanks for making the time."
"How are things on your end?"
When there's an audio or tech problem
This is the part that catches learners out — but there are standard phrases for it, and using them is completely normal: You can't hear them: "Sorry, you're breaking up — could you say that again?"
"I'm having trouble hearing you. Could you speak up a little?"
"I think the connection dropped for a second."
You didn't understand: "Sorry, could you repeat that?"
"Could you say that more slowly, please?"
"Just to confirm, you said…?"
Your own tech issues: "Can everyone hear me? I'm not sure my mic is working."
"My connection is unstable — I may drop off and rejoin."
"Let me turn my video off to help the connection."
Managing the moment: "Sorry, I think we talked over each other — please go ahead."
"You go first."
Asking someone to repeat or slow down is never rude on a call — everyone does it, and it's far better than guessing.
During the call
Stating the purpose: "The reason I'm calling is…" "There are a couple of things I'd like to go over."
Taking turns (harder without body language): "Can I jump in here?"
"Go ahead, [name]."
"I'll let you finish."
"Did you want to add anything?"
Checking and confirming: "Just to make sure we're on the same page…" "Could you clarify what you mean by…?"
"Let me repeat that back to you."
On video specifically: "I'll share my screen now — can you see it?"
"I'll put myself on mute while you talk."
"Sorry, I was on mute!" (a universal one) On calls, it helps to pause a beat before speaking so you don't talk over anyone — the slight audio delay makes overlaps common.
Ending the call
Wrapping up
"I think that covers everything — anything else before we finish?" "Thanks, that was really helpful."
Confirming next steps: "So just to confirm the next steps…" "I'll send a follow-up email with a summary."
"Let's catch up again next week."
"I'll get that over to you by [day]."
Signing off: "Thanks again for your time. Have a great day!"
"Great to talk — speak soon."
"Bye for now."
Ending with a clear summary of who does what by when is especially valuable on calls, where things are easy to mishear — it leaves no doubt about what was agreed.
Tips for calls as a non-native speaker
Keep key phrases visible. On a call, no one can see your notes — so keep a list of these phrases on-screen or beside you until they're automatic.

Slow down and speak clearly. Audio strips out some clarity, so crisp pronunciation and a slightly slower pace matter more on a call than in person. Don't fear the "repeat that" phrases. Using them is normal and professional, not a sign of weak English.
Prepare your opening and your purpose before you dial — the first 20 seconds are the most nerve-wracking.

The real challenge is that calls are audio-first — you can't rely on gestures — which is exactly why voice practice helps so much. With an AI speaking partner like Yappply, you practise in the same voice-only mode a call uses: you talk, it responds, and you get feedback on clarity and phrasing. Rehearsing calls this way — a quick role-play of answering the phone, handling a dropped connection, confirming next steps — makes the real ones feel routine. If calls are where your English feels hardest, voice practice is the most direct way to fix it.
Frequently asked questions

Why are English phone calls harder than talking in person? Because you lose body language and facial expressions that normally help you understand, and audio can be unclear or cut out. That makes clear language and ready phrases more important on calls. What do I say when I can't hear someone on a call? Use standard phrases like "Sorry, you're breaking up — could you say that again?" or "I'm having trouble hearing you, could you speak up a little?" These are completely normal on calls.

How do I answer a business phone call in English? "Hello, this is [name] speaking" or "[Company], [name] speaking — how can I help you?" Then listen, and use "The reason I'm calling is…" or ask how you can help.

Is it rude to ask someone to repeat or slow down on a call? No — it's normal and professional, and native speakers do it too. It's far better to ask than to guess and misunderstand something important.

How can I practise English for phone and video calls? Practise in voice-only mode: role- play answering a call, handling a dropped connection, and confirming next steps out loud. An AI speaking partner is ideal because it mirrors the audio-first nature of a real call and gives feedback.

title: How to Build Confidence Speaking English (7 Steps)
excerpt: Most learners wait to feel confident before they speak. That's the trap — confidence doesn't arrive first. Confidence is what your brain feels after it has evidence that speaking…
author: Salma Saleem

blocks.text: Most learners wait to feel confident before they speak. That's the trap — confidence doesn't arrive first. Confidence is what your brain feels after it has evidence that speaking went fine, so you build it by speaking, not by waiting. Each time you speak and get understood, your brain collects proof that it's safe, and the fear shrinks. The good news: confidence isn't tied to your level. You can be confident at a beginner level and anxious at an advanced one — it's about experience and mindset, not perfect grammar. These seven steps give you that experience in the right order, starting with practice so low-pressure you can do it alone today.
Why speaking English feels scary

Understanding the cause makes it easier to fix. The nerves almost always come from a few places: Fear of making mistakes. You worry about wrong grammar or pronunciation, so you edit every sentence before it leaves your mouth — and that self-monitoring is what causes the freeze.
Perfectionism. Waiting for the perfect sentence means you never start. Fluent communication values being understood over being flawless.
Comparing yourself to others. Measuring your speaking against native speakers or more advanced learners makes your own progress invisible.
Too little real practice. Years of reading and grammar but almost no speaking leaves your brain with no evidence that speaking is safe.
Past bad experiences. Being laughed at or corrected harshly once can make you avoid speaking, which keeps confidence low.
Notice that none of these are about your actual English ability. They're about mindset and reps — and both are fixable.

Start where no one is listening. Build your first reps in zero-pressure settings: read a page aloud, talk to yourself in the mirror, or describe your day out loud. You get used to the feeling of English in your mouth without anyone judging you. 2. Make peace with mistakes. Decide in advance that mistakes are normal and expected — even fluent speakers make them. Treat each one as data, not failure. The learners who improve fastest are the ones willing to be imperfect out loud. 3. Start simple and slow. Use short sentences and easy words, and speak a little more slowly than feels natural. Slowing down gives you time to think, cuts filler, and — counterintuitively — makes you sound more in control, not less.

Prepare go-to phrases. Have ready-made lines for the situations you face often: introducing yourself, buying something, starting a meeting. Phrases you can grab instantly ("to be honest," "could you repeat that?") give you a confident footing while you think.

Focus on the message, not on yourself. Shift your attention from "how do I sound" to "what am I trying to say" and to listening to the other person. When the goal is communication, not performance, the self-consciousness drops.

Practise every day to stack evidence. Short daily speaking — even five minutes — beats a long session once a week. Each successful rep is a brick of proof that speaking is safe, and confidence is built brick by brick.

Track your small wins. Record yourself occasionally and compare across weeks, or note moments that went well ("I ordered food without freezing"). Seeing your own progress is the fuel that keeps the confidence loop going.
A 10-minute daily confidence routine

Confidence compounds when the reps are small and regular. Try this: The rule that matters most: speak even when you're nervous, and don't stop to fix mistakes mid-sentence. Every time you push through, you teach your brain that speaking is safe — and that's what confidence is made of.
The safest place to practise: no judgment

Almost every step above needs the same thing — a space where you can speak daily and make mistakes without anyone judging you. That's exactly what holds most learners back: speaking to real people feels risky, so they never get the reps that build confidence. An AI speaking partner removes the fear. You can have a real conversation any time, on any topic, make as many mistakes as you need, and get gentle, instant feedback — with no one watching. It's the judgment-free, daily practice this whole process depends on, and it lets you stack those small wins fast. If nerves are what stop you from speaking English, practising with an AI partner is the lowest-pressure way to build the evidence your confidence is waiting for.
Frequently asked questions

How can I speak English confidently without hesitation? Start in low-pressure settings, use short simple sentences, and don't stop to fix mistakes mid-sentence. Hesitation drops as you get daily reps and your brain learns that speaking is safe. Minutes What to do What it builds
0–2 Read a short passage aloud, slowly and clearly Comfort with English out loud 2–5 Answer one question about your day in full sentences, no stopping for mistakes Fluency under light pressure
5–7 Practise 2–3 go-to phrases for a situation you'll face this week Ready footing for real moments 7–9 Record the answer and note one thing that went well Evidence of progress
9–10 Write down one small win from today Reinforces the confidence loop

Why do I lose confidence even though I know English? Because confidence comes from speaking experience, not knowledge. You can know a lot of grammar and vocabulary but still freeze if you rarely practise speaking out loud. The fix is reps, not more study. Do I need perfect grammar to sound confident? No. Confident speakers make small mistakes all the time. Being understood matters far more than being perfect, and fluency plus a calm delivery reads as confidence even when the grammar isn't flawless. How long does it take to feel more confident speaking English? Many learners feel a noticeable shift within a few weeks of daily speaking practice, as small wins accumulate. It's gradual, but the early progress comes fast once you start speaking every day. What's the fastest way to build speaking confidence? Daily, low-pressure speaking practice with feedback — whether talking to yourself, a patient friend, or an AI partner — so you collect steady evidence that speaking goes fine.

title: 100 English Conversation Topics With Questions (All Levels)
excerpt: The hardest part of practising English speaking is often just finding something to talk about. This is a ready-made library of conversation topics, each with questions you can…
author: Salma Saleem

blocks.text: The hardest part of practising English speaking is often just finding something to talk about. This is a ready-made library of conversation topics, each with questions you can answer right away — grouped by level and by situation.

How to use it: pick a topic, answer all its questions out loud in full sentences, then push one answer further with a "why" or "for example." Don't just think the answers — say them. Speaking out loud is what builds fluency. Start at your level, and move up when the questions feel easy. You can do these alone, with a partner, or with an AI speaking partner.
Beginner topics (A1–A2)
Start here if you can make simple sentences. These stay concrete — your own life, in the present, past, and near future.
Daily routine: What time do you wake up? What do you do in the morning? What's your favourite part of the day?
Family: How many people are in your family? Who are you closest to? What do you do together?
Food: What did you eat today? What's your favourite dish? Can you cook? What do you want to try?

Home: Where do you live? What's your favourite room? What's near your home? Hobbies: What do you do in your free time? How did you start? Who do you do it with? Weather & seasons: What's the weather like today? What's your favourite season? What do you do when it rains?
Work or study: What do you do? What do you like about it? What's a normal day like? Friends: Who is your best friend? How did you meet? What do you like to do together?
Intermediate topics (B1–B2)

For these, give opinions and reasons, not just facts. Aim for 3–4 sentences per answer. Travel: What's the best place you've visited? How do you prefer to travel? Where would you go with unlimited money, and why?
Technology: How has your phone changed your life? Could you live without social media? Is technology making us closer or more distant?
Health & fitness: How do you stay healthy? Has your lifestyle changed over the years? What habit would you like to build?
Money: Do you prefer saving or spending? What's worth paying more for? How do you decide on a big purchase?
Education: What was your favourite subject and why? Is it better to learn online or in a classroom? What skill do you wish schools taught?
City life: What do you like about where you live? City or countryside — which suits you? How has your city changed?
Entertainment: What do you watch or listen to? How do you choose what's worth your time? Has what you enjoy changed as you've got older?
Work: What makes a good manager? Would you prefer to work from home or an office? What does your ideal job look like?
Advanced topics (C1–C2)
These are abstract — argue a position, weigh both sides, and use linking language to structure your thoughts.

Society: Is society becoming more or less equal? What social change would you most like to see? Do individuals or governments do more to shape a country? Culture: How does culture shape the way people communicate? Is globalisation good or bad for local traditions? What does your culture value most?
Career & success: How do you define success? Is passion or stability more important in a career? Will AI change the jobs of the future — and how?
Environment: Who is most responsible for solving climate change? Would you give up conveniences to help the planet? Are individual actions enough?
Ethics & choices: Is it ever acceptable to break a rule? Should some things never be for sale? How do you make a hard decision?
The future: What will daily life look like in 30 years? Are you optimistic or pessimistic about the future? What technology worries you?
Values: What matters more — freedom or security? Has social media changed what we value? What advice would you give your younger self?
Topics by situation
Sometimes you need language for a specific moment. Practise these the way you'll actually use them.
Small talk: How was your weekend? Any plans for the holidays? Did you see the game / the news? How's work going?

At work & in meetings: Can you give a quick update on your project? What do you think we should prioritise? Could you clarify that point? I'd like to add something here. Job interviews: Tell me about yourself. Why do you want this role? What are your strengths? Where do you see yourself in five years?
Making friends: What do you do for fun? How long have you lived here? Have you seen anything good lately? We should do this again sometime.

Travelling abroad: Could you recommend somewhere to eat? How do I get to the station? Do you have this in a different size? Could you help me — I'm a bit lost. For each situation, imagine the real setting and say your answers out loud as if the other person were there.
How to keep the conversation going
Topics get you started; these habits keep you talking
Always give a reason. After your answer, add "because…" It naturally doubles the length of what you say.

Add an example. "For instance…" turns a short answer into a real one. Bounce it back. End with "What about you?" to keep a real conversation flowing. Don't aim for perfect. Keep going even with small mistakes — fluency comes from not stopping.

The key is to practise these out loud, every day. Reading the questions silently does nothing; speaking the answers builds the skill. If you don't have someone to talk to, an AI speaking partner like Yappply lets you work through topics like these in real conversations any time, and gives you feedback on how you did — turning this list into daily speaking practice that actually sticks.
Frequently asked questions

What are good English conversation topics for beginners? Concrete, personal topics work best: daily routine, family, food, home, hobbies, and the weather. Each lets you build simple sentences about things you already know.

How do I practice English conversation topics alone? Pick a topic, answer every question out loud in full sentences, then push one answer further with a reason or example. Record yourself to check your fluency, or use an AI speaking partner to practise them as real conversations.

How many questions should I answer per topic? Answer all the questions under a topic, then add your own follow-ups. Quality of speaking time matters more than the number — aim for 5–10 minutes of talking.

What topics come up in English speaking exams and interviews? Familiar ones: work or study, hometown, hobbies, and opinions on everyday issues. The "by situation" section above covers interview and small-talk questions directly.
How often should I practise with these topics? Daily, even for 10–15 minutes. A different topic each day keeps practice fresh and builds a wide range of vocabulary over time.

title: Common English Phrases for Office Meetings
excerpt: Speaking up in an English meeting can feel intimidating — you know what you want to say, but finding the right words fast enough is hard. The good news: meetings follow…
author: Salma Saleem

blocks.text: Speaking up in an English meeting can feel intimidating — you know what you want to say, but finding the right words fast enough is hard. The good news: meetings follow predictable moments — opening, giving an opinion, agreeing, disagreeing, clarifying, and wrapping up — so if you learn a few ready-made phrases for each, you'll always have something professional to say.

Think of these as building blocks you can grab instantly, so your energy goes into your idea rather than scrambling for words. Below are the most useful phrases, grouped by the moment you'll need them.
Starting the meeting and giving updates
To open or get started
"Thanks everyone for joining. Shall we get started?"
"Today I'd like to cover three things…" "Let's begin with the first item on the agenda."
To give your update
"I'll give you a quick update on…" "Where we are right now is…" "The main progress since last time is…" "One thing I want to flag is…"
To hand over
"That's it from me — I'll pass it over to [name]."
"I'd be happy to go into more detail if useful."
Giving opinions, agreeing, and disagreeing
To give your opinion
"In my opinion…" / "From my point of view…" "I think we should…" "What I'd suggest is…"
To agree
"I completely agree."
"That's a good point."
"Yes, exactly — and I'd add that…"
To disagree politely (the key word is politely — soften it)
"I see your point, but…" "I'm not sure I agree, because…" "That's one option, though another way to look at it is…" "I'd push back on that slightly — what about…?"
Disagreeing in English usually starts by acknowledging the other person first. Jumping straight to "No, you're wrong" sounds harsh; "I see your point, but…" keeps it professional.
Interrupting and clarifying
To interrupt politely
"Sorry to jump in, but…" "Can I add something here?"
"Just quickly on that point…"
Common English Phrases for Oﬃce Meetings
To ask for clarification (never pretend you understood — asking is normal and professional): "Sorry, could you clarify what you mean by…?"
"Just to make sure I understand — are you saying…?"
"Could you give an example?"
"Sorry, could you repeat that last part?"
To check others understood you
"Does that make sense?"
"Let me know if I should explain that differently."
"Are we all on the same page?"
If you miss something, ask. Everyone — native speakers included — asks people to repeat things in meetings.
Making suggestions and wrapping up
To make a suggestion
"Why don't we…?"
"How about we…?"

"It might be worth…" "One option would be to…" To respond to a question: "Good question. The short answer is…" "I'd need to check, but my understanding is…" "Let me come back to you on that." (perfect when you need time) To wrap up and set action items: "So, to summarise…" "The key takeaways are…" "Let's agree on next steps."
"[Name], could you take the lead on…?"
"Let's follow up on this by [day]."
"Thanks everyone — I'll send a summary afterwards."
"Let me come back to you on that" is especially useful: it's a professional way to buy time instead of panicking when you're put on the spot.

Speaking up with confidence

Knowing the phrases is half the battle; using them smoothly is the other half. A few tips: Prepare one or two points before the meeting and the phrase you'll use to raise them, so you're not composing under pressure.
Speak early. The longer you wait to say your first thing, the harder it gets. A quick "That's a good point" in the first few minutes breaks the ice.
Keep it short. You don't need long, complex sentences — a clear, short contribution lands better than a rambling one.
Rehearse the phrases out loud until they come automatically, so they're ready when the moment arrives.

Frequently asked questions

How can I speak more confidently in English meetings? Learn ready-made phrases for each moment (opening, giving opinions, disagreeing, clarifying, wrapping up), prepare a point or two in advance, and speak early. Having phrases ready means you focus on your idea, not on finding words.

How do I disagree politely in a meeting in English? Acknowledge the other person first, then give your view: "I see your point, but…" or "That's one option, though another way to look at it is…" Jumping straight to "you're wrong" sounds harsh in English. What do I say when I don't understand something in a meeting? Ask — it's normal and professional. Use "Sorry, could you clarify what you mean by…?" or "Just to make sure I understand, are you saying…?"
What can I say when I'm put on the spot and need time? "Let me come back to you on that" or "I'd need to check, but my understanding is…" Both buy you time professionally instead of panicking.

How do I practise English for meetings? Role-play the situations out loud — giving an update, disagreeing, answering a question — until the phrases come automatically. A partner or an AI speaking app that can role-play meetings is ideal for this.
